strengths: Technically sound and well-executed core contribution: the block-sparse correlation volume sampler exactly matches the RAFT mathematical operator (verified by unit tests and a near-zero 0.03% EPE difference), so it is a drop-in replacement with no accuracy compromise — this is the right way to claim an efficiency contribution.

Strong empirical evidence for the efficiency claims: isolated benchmarks (Fig. 5, Table 6) show up to ~90% runtime improvement over on-demand sampling and ~96% memory reduction vs. the dense default, consistent across four GPU models; end-to-end results in Table 3 confirm substantial speedups for RAFT, CCMR, MS-RAFT+ and SEA-RAFT at UHR scales.

The analysis in Sec. 3.2 (only ~1.6% of the volume is sampled; patch-major layout roughly halves required blocks at B=8, Table 4) and the O(n^1.5) memory complexity derivation (supplementary Eq. 3) provide a well-motivated and reproducible foundation for the design decisions.

The 8K CHARGE-based dataset addresses a real gap: no prior reference-based benchmark exists at ultra-high resolution, and the paper is transparent about generation details (renderer settings, script in Listing 1, sequence list), supporting reproducibility.

The cascaded test-time extension of SEA-RAFT is a simple but effective contribution: it reduces large-motion EPE substantially (e.g., 107.39 -> 21.56 px at 1/1) without retraining, and achieves the best 1px outlier rate and LM-EPE on the new benchmark (Table 2).
Evaluation breadth is good: ablations over iterations, feature dimensionality, block size, and hardware, plus runtime measurements on Sintel, KITTI, and Spring.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: block-sparse computation with tiling, caching across iterations, and layout reorganization are largely systems-level optimizations in the spirit of FlashAttention/Neighborhood Attention rather than a new algorithmic idea; the paper is careful not to overclaim this, but reviewers seeking deeper novelty may find the contribution incremental.

The new 8K benchmark is small and narrow: only 335 frames from 3 sequences of a single movie, forward flow only. Conclusions about UHR behavior (e.g., that native-resolution inference generally helps but harms large-displacement estimation) rest on very limited scene diversity, and there is no discussion of data licensing/distribution.

The 'similar memory as on-demand sampling' claim (Sec. 6.3) is overstated in places: Table 3 shows Ours can use substantially more memory than on-demand at 8192px (e.g., RAFT 19.42 vs 19.40 is on par, but SEA-RAFT 17.21 vs 10.25 GiB and MS-RAFT+ 53.92 vs 24.22 GiB are far above), largely due to caching overhead.

At low/native benchmark resolutions the method offers little or no benefit and is sometimes slower (Tables 8-10: -4% to -23% for some methods, +0% for others), so the practical impact is concentrated in the UHR regime the authors themselves introduce; the accuracy SOTA claim on that benchmark is partially self-referential (own dataset, own cascade extension).

The claimed benefit that higher-resolution inference reconstructs fine details better is mostly supported qualitatively (Fig. 6); quantitative detail metrics are deferred to the supplementary material and are not clearly summarized in the main paper.
Accuracy evaluations on Sintel/KITTI use training splits rather than the official test servers, which limits comparability with the literature, although this is acknowledged.

Some overhead remains (Table 1: mask setting, block indices, cache updating consume up to ~72% of runtime at 1024px), which the authors acknowledge; the operator is not yet competitive at low resolution, and further kernel optimization is left to future work.

strengths: The core technical idea is sound and well-motivated: the empirical analysis of correlation volume access patterns (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 3) showing only ~1.6% of cells are sampled, and the observation that a patch-major layout dramatically increases block sparsity (Table 4), provides a clear and credible foundation for the block-sparse sampling algorithm.

The method exactly preserves the RAFT operator semantics, with correctness validated via unit tests and a reported 0.03% endpoint error difference against the official implementation, so the efficiency gains come without any quality compromise.

The evaluation is thorough: isolated operator benchmarks across four GPUs, multiple resolutions, iteration counts, and feature dimensionalities (Figs. 5, 7-9, Table 6), an honest runtime breakdown (Table 1) that acknowledges substantial overheads in mask/caching steps, and ablations of the caching mechanism.
The supplementary material is substantive rather than superficial, including pseudocode (Algorithm 1), a memory complexity derivation showing O(P^1.5) space, and full per-dataset result tables.

Releasing an 8K ground-truth flow benchmark (332 pairs, 9.3B pixels) addresses a real evaluation gap, since existing benchmarks stop at HD resolution, and the systematic study of accuracy vs. processing scale across 13 methods (Tables 2, 7) is a useful community resource.
weaknesses: The novelty is primarily at the systems/engineering level. Block-sparse computation of a mostly-unused matrix, caching across iterations, and patch-major memory layouts are individually well-known techniques; the contribution is their careful combination and CUDA implementation for one specific operator. There is limited methodological insight beyond 'only compute the blocks that are sampled'.

The headline gains are partly an artifact of the comparison regime. The up-to-90%/58%/27% improvements are against the on-demand baseline or measured at resolutions where alternatives go out-of-memory; on standard-resolution benchmarks (Tables 8-10), the method frequently makes things worse: SEA-RAFT is -23% on Spring, CCMR+ is -15% on Spring and -12% on KITTI, MS-RAFT+ is -21%/-23%. The practical benefit is confined to a narrow UHR regime.

Memory claims are less favorable than the abstract suggests. In Table 3, 'Ours' can consume substantially more memory than on-demand sampling and even than the default (e.g., CCMR at 8192: 66.68 GiB vs. 36.30 GiB on-demand; SEA-RAFT at 8192: 17.21 vs. 10.25 GiB), and Table 1 shows ~50% of runtime at low resolution is spent on non-compute mask/cache bookkeeping. The caching threshold (5GB over-allocation) is a heuristic that is not ablated.

The new 8K dataset is small and narrow: 332 evaluation pairs from only 3 sequences of a single synthetic Blender movie, forward flow only, and derived from content that also appears in prior flow benchmarks. Claims of 'state-of-the-art at 8K' rest on this very limited evaluation; generalization of the large-motion conclusions to real UHR footage is unverified.

The cascaded inference extension (Sec. 6.2) is a simple test-time multi-resolution warm start; it is a reasonable trick but thin as a contribution, and its hyperparameter (the 800px threshold, 1/4 downscale) is presented without sensitivity analysis.

Several important details are deferred entirely to supplementary material (block size selection rationale, full numerical sampling statistics, dataset generation), leaving the main paper thin on justification of key design constants such as B=8 vs. B=16 being used inconsistently across methods.
No explicit statement about public release of code or the dataset is present; given that the dataset is the main reusable artifact, reproducibility of the benchmark claims is uncertain.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the quadratic memory cost of dense all-pairs correlation volumes versus the poor runtime of on-demand sampling is a genuine practical limitation for ultra-high-resolution (UHR) optical flow, and the paper positions itself precisely between these two existing implementations.

The core idea is grounded in empirical analysis rather than intuition: the access-pattern study (Fig. 3, Sec. 3.2, Table 4) showing only ~1.6% of volume cells are sampled, and the observation that patch-major layout increases block sparsity at no cost, directly motivate the block-sparse design.

The algorithm matches the exact RAFT operator (verified at 0.03% endpoint error difference), making it a credible drop-in replacement rather than an approximation; the O(n^1.5) memory derivation in the supplementary is a useful theoretical addition.

Extensive and careful evaluation: isolated operator benchmarks across resolutions, feature dimensionalities, iteration counts, and four GPU models (Table 6, Figs. 5, 7-9); end-to-end integration into five RAFT-family methods (Table 3); and additional runtime results on Spring, Sintel, and KITTI.

The contribution bundle is substantial beyond the operator: a new 8K benchmark (Charge-based, 335 frames with 16K super-resolved ground truth, generation script included) and a training-free cascaded inference extension of SEA-RAFT that reduces large-motion EPE substantially (e.g., 1/1 scale EPE from 17.63 to 2.70, Table 7).

Honest reporting of overheads: the component breakdown (Table 1) transparently shows that mask setup and cache updates dominate at low resolution, and the conclusion acknowledges the lack of low-level kernel optimization.
weaknesses: The empirical foundation for sparsity (1.6% sampled cells, Table 4) is measured only on Sintel, a relatively low-resolution dataset with small motions. At native 8K resolution, where the paper motivates its method, flow magnitudes and the fraction of sampled blocks could differ substantially; no sparsity statistics are reported on the UHR data itself.

The 8K benchmark is narrow: 335 frames from a single synthetic Blender movie (3 shots), forward flow only. While consistent with Spring's methodology, it is a small and domain-limited evaluation basis for 'state-of-the-art at 8K' claims, and the compared methods use checkpoints trained on Sintel/KITTI, which the authors themselves note makes some error measurements unrepresentative.

Several headline numbers are best-case figures: 'up to 90%' over on-demand sampling, 'up to 58%' end-to-end, 'up to 95%' memory savings. Table 3 shows more mixed outcomes for some method/resolution combinations (e.g., CCMR at 8192 is only 15% faster and uses 66.68 GiB vs. 36.30 GiB for on-demand, and gains on Spring/KITTI/Sintel are small or negative for several methods).

At low and moderate resolutions the added bookkeeping overhead means the method offers little or no runtime benefit over the default dense implementation (Table 1: 44.7 ms vs. presumably faster dense compute; Tables 8-10 show 0% to -23% differences), so the practical impact is confined to high-resolution, memory-constrained settings; the paper could state this trade-off more prominently.

The cascaded inference heuristic (downscale at 1/4 whenever min dimension > 800px) is somewhat ad hoc; the choice of threshold and scaling factors is not ablated, and no comparison is made against alternative training-free coarse-to-fine initialization strategies.

Peak memory measurements show large variance in places (e.g., 2926 ± 1023 MB at 4096 width, Table 6), and the caching growth policy (5GB headroom, growth factor 2) introduces implementation-dependent memory behavior that is described but not systematically ablated.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'qualitative evaluation' for Table 7 which is quantitative, 'an example of from the dataset', 'renders several sequences' phrasing), though these do not impede understanding.
